browsecomp.reading: A correct short answer earns the point; the score does not tell you whether the agent can write a well-supported research report.
browsecomp.contrast: finish a transaction or change a website, rather than find an answer.

facts.label: What the model submits
facts.value: A short factual answer, not a research report.

osworld.reading: Opening the right application is not enough: if the requested file or setting is still unchanged, the agent has not completed the task.
osworld.contrast: coordinate applications through tools rather than desktop controls.

apex-agents.reading: A deliverable can satisfy most rubric criteria and still fail the task: mean score gives partial credit, while Pass@1 requires the whole rubric.
apex-agents.contrast: compare a finished deliverable with a professional’s work.

arc-agi-3.reading: Two agents can clear the same levels and score differently: actions spent discovering the rules count against efficiency relative to humans.
arc-agi-3.contrast: infer the rule from static examples, without interacting with an environment.

arc-agi-2.reading: A nearly right transformation still misses the task if the output grid has the wrong shape or even one wrong cell.
arc-agi-2.contrast: test how efficiently an agent discovers rules by acting.

humaneval.reading: Pass@k asks whether at least one of k candidate functions passes the tests; compare pass@1 when a user only gets the first answer.
humaneval.contrast: repair an existing repository instead of writing an isolated function.

swe-bench.reading: A patch need not match the maintainer’s code: it must fix the targeted failures without breaking the designated regression tests.
swe-bench.contrast: test function writing without repository navigation.

terminal-bench.reading: The verifier checks what the commands leave behind, so a plausible shell transcript is not evidence that the task succeeded.
terminal-bench.contrast: require an analysis or simulation to meet scientific checks.

terminal-bench-science.reading: A workflow can run to completion and still fail if its output misses a scientific check; the score measures delivery of a defined result, not selection of a research question.
terminal-bench-science.contrast: reproduce a paper and its experiments rather than finish one assigned workflow.

facts.label: What gets checked
facts.value: The resulting artifact: an analysis, simulation, proof or other research output.

paperbench.reading: A replication score of 50% means half the weighted rubric credit, not that half the papers were reproduced in full.
paperbench.contrast: measure research engineering progress against experts on a time budget.

re-bench.reading: The time budget can change which side leads: the original study found different human–agent comparisons at two hours and at eight.
re-bench.contrast: replicate a paper instead of optimizing a task metric.

toolathlon.reading: A sequence of valid tool calls can still score zero if it leaves the applications in the wrong state.
toolathlon.contrast: test operating a desktop rather than making tool calls.

webarena.reading: The agent uses functional websites to finish assigned tasks; despite the name, users are not voting on which website looks better.
webarena.contrast: find a fact on the open web instead of changing a website.

gdpval.reading: A win means a professional preferred the model’s deliverable to the human comparison; it is not a measure of the share of a job the model can do.
gdpval.contrast: grade multi-step work inside a professional workspace.

graphwalks.reading: The answer is a set of nodes reached by following edges: spotting one relevant line in a long prompt will not solve a multi-hop query.
graphwalks.contrast: test retrieval of a planted fact without graph traversal.

needle-in-a-haystack.reading: In the single-needle test, a hit shows the model recovered one planted fact at that length and position—not that it connected evidence across the document.
needle-in-a-haystack.contrast: follow relationships across the input rather than retrieve one item.

healthbench.reading: Physicians wrote the rubrics; a model grades each response. The score is not the share of answers approved by a doctor.

deepswe.reading: A change that works only in the agent’s workspace can fail: v1.1 applies the committed patch in a clean environment before grading.

aa-intelligence-index.reading: Compare scores from the same index version. A change in tasks, graders or weights can move the number without any change to the model.
aa-intelligence-index.contrast: inspect separate scenario metrics instead of a composite ranking.

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: Knowledge work, coding, science and general tasks.

facts.label: Test access
facts.value: Some component tests or answers are held out.

code-arena-webdev.reading: A higher rating means users preferred those apps in this pool of matchups. It is not the percentage of the brief implemented correctly.
code-arena-webdev.contrast: test an agent using a website, rather than building one.

facts.label: Evaluation
facts.value: Live head-to-head votes, not a fixed test set.

gamecraft-bench.reading: No launch or usable replay means zero credit. A high score shows the requested gameplay was demonstrated, not that players enjoyed it.
gamecraft-bench.contrast: ask people which generated web app they prefer, rather than score a Godot replay.

chatbot-arena.reading: Ratings reflect which response people preferred in anonymous matchups, not the proportion of prompts answered correctly.
chatbot-arena.contrast: compare working web apps rather than chat responses.
